items.headline: Ultragenyx prices Sanfilippo gene therapy at $4M; Bristol Myers shelves Orum drug
items.preview: Ultragenyx's Fayuvi gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome is priced at $3.95 million. Bristol Myers has halted development of ORM-6151.
items.article:
The FDA has approved Fayuvi, the first gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome Type A, priced at $3.95 million. This marks Ultragenyx's second gene therapy approval since August, although analysts do not expect blockbuster sales. The company has warned of upcoming cost cuts following the failure of another drug. 
Bristol Myers Squibb has ceased development of ORM-6151, an experimental cancer drug, after reviewing Phase 1 trial data. The company had previously invested $100 million for the rights to the therapy, which was aimed at treating acute myeloid leukemia. 
Why this matters: The approval of Fayuvi represents a significant milestone in gene therapy for rare diseases, while the shelving of ORM-6151 highlights the challenges in drug development.

items.headline: Ultragenyx wins first approval for MPS IIIA, closing a bumpy four-year path
items.preview: Ultragenyx has received FDA approval for Fayuvi, the first treatment for Sanfilippo syndrome Type A.
items.article:
Ultragenyx has secured FDA approval for rebisufligene etisparvovec, now known as Fayuvi, marking the first treatment for Sanfilippo syndrome Type A. This approval concludes a challenging four-year regulatory journey for the company. 
The FDA's decision reflects a traditional approval based on clinical evidence rather than the previously sought accelerated approval, indicating a significant step forward in the treatment of this rare disease. 
Why this matters: This approval not only provides a new treatment option for patients but also sets a precedent for future gene therapies in rare diseases.

items.headline: Discovery of CRISPR's long lost ancestor may expand gene-editing toolkit
items.preview: Researchers have identified a precursor to CRISPR that could enhance gene-editing technologies.
items.article:
Recent studies have uncovered a precursor to CRISPR, an RNA-guided system found in viruses, which may expand the gene-editing toolkit. This discovery sheds light on the evolutionary origins of CRISPR systems, which have been pivotal in gene editing. 
The research indicates that this ancient system, called VIPR, could lead to new programmable genetic tools, enhancing the capabilities of current CRISPR technologies. 
Why this matters: Understanding the origins of CRISPR could inspire innovative approaches to gene editing, potentially leading to more versatile and effective applications in medicine and agriculture.

items.headline: Virtual biotech company puts thousands of AI scientist agents to work on drug discovery
items.preview: A new virtual biotech company utilizes 37,000 AI agents to streamline drug discovery processes.
items.article:
A virtual biotech company has been established, employing 37,000 AI agents to facilitate drug discovery without human intervention. This innovative approach aims to tackle the complexities of drug development from target identification to clinical trial design. 
The AI agents have already demonstrated the ability to uncover biological signals that predict drug success and have designed a cancer therapy that has garnered interest from a major pharmaceutical company. 
Why this matters: This model represents a significant shift in drug discovery, potentially reducing costs and time associated with traditional methods.

items.headline: Collagen I promotes cancer cell survival via amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activation
items.preview: New research reveals how collagen I supports cancer cell survival under nutrient deprivation.
items.article:
Recent findings indicate that collagen I is crucial for the survival of breast and pancreatic cancer cells, particularly under glucose starvation conditions. The study demonstrates that collagen I activates mTORC1 signaling, promoting amino acid import and limiting autophagy. 
Inhibition of the integrin or amino acid transporter involved in this process significantly reduces cancer cell growth and invasion. The research highlights the potential of targeting these pathways as a therapeutic strategy in fibrotic and nutrient-deprived tumors. 
Why this matters: Understanding the role of collagen I in cancer metabolism could lead to new treatment strategies aimed at improving patient outcomes in aggressive cancers.
